pl-l3d6c6-d1e114.summary: Continues Augustine: some things that come to make a habitus are not changed but change what they come to, as wisdom changes a fool into a wise man.
claims: Some accruing things change without being changed.

pl-l3d6c6-d1e120.summary: Gives the second kind: some things come so as both to change and be changed, as food loses its form, turns into the body, and restores us from weakness to strength.
claims: Some accruing things both change and are changed.

pl-l3d6c6-d1e126.summary: Gives the third kind: some things neither change what they come to nor are changed by it, as a ring on a finger, a very rare kind.
claims: Some accruing things neither change nor are changed.

pl-l3d6c6-d1e132.summary: Gives the fourth kind, which fits the incarnation: things that come and are changed not in nature but in shape, like a garment that takes the form of the limbs when worn. So the Son of God emptied himself, not changing his own form but taking the form of a servant, not converted into man but made in the likeness of men by truly assuming man, and found 'in habitus as a man', i.e., by having a man, not to himself but to those to whom he appeared. 'As a man' expresses truth.
claims: The incarnation is like a garment shaped by the wearer.
The Son emptied himself without changing his divine form.
'As a man' signifies true humanity.

pl-l3d6c6-d1e154.summary: Concludes Augustine: by 'habitus' the Apostle showed that he was made in the likeness of men not by transfiguration into man but by clothing himself in man, whom, uniting and conforming to himself, he joined to immortality and eternity. The Word was not changed by assuming man, as limbs are not changed by clothing, though that assumption ineffably joined the assumed to the assumer.
claims: The Word was not changed by assuming man.
The assumption ineffably joined the assumed to the assumer.

pl-l3d6c6-d1e163.summary: Observes that these words of Augustine clearly seem to suggest that God is said to be made man by habitus.
claims: Augustine seems to teach that God is made man by habitus.

pl-l3d6c6-d1e169.summary: Cites Augustine, De Trinitate IV, on how the incarnation was done: the Word was made flesh, i.e., man, not converted or changed, but clothed in flesh to appear fittingly to carnal men; and not only flesh but a rational soul, so that the whole is called God because of God and man because of man. If this is hard to understand, the mind must be purified by faith, abstaining from sin and doing good.
claims: The Word was clothed in flesh without change.
The whole is called God because of God and man because of man.
Understanding the incarnation requires a mind purified by faith.

pl-l3d6c6-d1e184.summary: Cites Augustine, De fide ad Petrum: the eternal Son became for us true and full man: true because he has true human nature, full because he took human flesh and rational soul.
claims: Christ is true man by true human nature and full man by flesh and rational soul.

pl-l3d6c6-d1e193.summary: Adds from the same work: the emptying of the highest God was nothing but the taking of the form of a servant, i.e., human nature. So both forms are in Christ, since both substances, divine and human, are true and full in him.
claims: Kenosis is the assumption of human nature.
Both forms, divine and human, are true and full in Christ.

pl-l3d6c6-d1e199.summary: Cites Augustine, Contra Maximinum: invisible in himself, he appeared visible in the man he deigned to take from a woman.
claims: The invisible God appeared visibly in the assumed man.

pl-l3d6c6-d1e209.summary: Adds from the same work: we believe Christ took true man and in him appeared visibly, lived among men, suffered human things from men, and taught men.
claims: Christ acted and suffered in the man he assumed.

pl-l3d6c6-d1e218.summary: Cites Hilary, De Trinitate X: the Son of God was born of Mary because the Word was made flesh, taking the form of a servant while in the form of God; we confess one and the same, not by God's failing but by assuming man, in the form of God by divine nature and found in the form of a servant according to the habitus of a man. That habitus was not of a man but as of a man, and the flesh not of sin but in the likeness of sinful flesh.
claims: Christ is one in both forms.
He is found in the form of a servant according to the habitus of a man.
concepts: form of God and form of a servant

pl-l3d6c6-d1e248.summary: Concludes: three opinions held by different people have been set out, with testimonies for each.

pl-l3d6c6.summary: Continues Augustine's 83 Questions on the kinds of habitus: things that come and change others without being changed (wisdom), things that change and are changed (food), things that neither change nor are changed (a ring), and things that are changed not in nature but in shape (clothing). The last fits the incarnation: the Son emptied himself, not changing his form but taking a servant's form, found 'as a man' by having a man, to those to whom he appeared. So the Word was not changed by assuming man, as limbs are not changed by clothing. Further texts of Augustine (De Trinitate IV, De fide ad Petrum, Contra Maximinum) and Hilary are adduced. Lombard closes: three opinions have been set out with their authorities.
claims: The incarnation is like the fourth kind of habitus, a garment shaped by the wearer.
The Word was not changed by assuming man.
Christ was found 'as a man' by having a man.
Christ has both forms, divine and human, true and complete.
